## `palmerpenguins` dataset

Size measurements, clutch observations, and blood isotope ratios for adult foraging Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins observed on islands in the Palmer Archipelago near Palmer Station, Antarctica. Data were collected and made available by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) Program.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#load data 
library(palmerpenguins) 
data(penguins)         
```

## `drop_na()`

`drop_na()` removes rows with missing data. If you use it with no additional arguments it will drop a row that contains an `NA` in any column.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# save as new object
# drop_na without pipe

penguins_mod <- drop_na(penguins)

# drop_na with pipe

penguins_mod <- penguins |>
  drop_na()
```
:::




::: callout-warning
Is it appropriate to remove rows with missing data? How many rows have missing data? Do the missing rows have something in common?

Removing rows can affect the validity and generalizability of your analysis!
:::

## `summarize()` or `summarise()` (either works)

Suppose we are interested in the average bill length of all Adelie penguins.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use summarize for average bill length in Adelie penguins
# Do it first without removing NAs

penguins |>
  filter(species=="Adelie") |>
  summarize(mean(bill_length_mm))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  `mean(bill_length_mm)`
                   <dbl>
1                     NA
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# have to deal with the NAs

penguins |>
  filter(species=="Adelie") |>
  summarize(mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  `mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)`
                                 <dbl>
1                                 38.8
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Then remove NAs using na.rm=TRUE


penguins |>
  filter(species=="Adelie") |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm)  |>
  summarize(mean(bill_length_mm))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  `mean(bill_length_mm)`
                   <dbl>
1                   38.8
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  filter(species=="Adelie") |>
  drop_na() |>
  summarize(mean(bill_length_mm))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  `mean(bill_length_mm)`
                   <dbl>
1                   38.8
```


:::
:::




Suppose we are interested in the average bill length AND average bill depth of all Adelie penguins:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# calculate average bill length and average bill depth for Adelie
# filter for Adelie then summarize

penguins |>
  filter(species=="Adelie") |>
  summarize(mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE),
            mean(bill_depth_mm, na.rm=TRUE))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  `mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)` `mean(bill_depth_mm, na.rm = TRUE)`
                                 <dbl>                               <dbl>
1                                 38.8                                18.3
```


:::
:::




There are lots of other functions available:

-   `min`: minimum value
-   `max`: maximum value
-   `mean`: average or mean value
-   `median`: median value
-   `var`: variance
-   `sd`: standard deviation
-   `n`: count or number of values
-   `n_distinct`: counts number of distinct values

Suppose we are interested in the average bill length AND the median bill length of all Adelie penguins:

```{.r .cell-code}
  summarize(mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE),
            median(bill_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE),
            n())
```

## `group_by()`

Let's say we were interested in the average bill length and bill depth of all penguin species in this dataset. We could repeat this for the other species (Gentoo and Chinstrap). This would be a fair amount of work AND the results would not end up in the same table.

OR we could use the `group_by` command!




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# group_by species and then summarize bill length and bill depth (mean)


penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm) |>
  summarize(mean_bill_length=mean(bill_length_mm),
            mean_bill_depth=mean(bill_depth_mm))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   mean_bill_length mean_bill_depth
  <fct>                <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Adelie                38.8            18.3
2 Chinstrap             48.8            18.4
3 Gentoo                47.5            15.0
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  group_by(island) |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm) |>
  summarize(mean_bill_length=mean(bill_length_mm),
            mean_bill_depth=mean(bill_depth_mm))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

  island    mean_bill_length mean_bill_depth
  <fct>                <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Biscoe                45.3            15.9

3 Torgersen             39.0            18.4
```

## `mutate()`

`mutate()` creates new columns that are functions of existing variables.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# first just create a new column that contains all 5s

penguins_mod <- penguins |>
  mutate(fives=5)
```
:::




For example, let's calculate create a new column which displays the body length weight in pounds (lbs) instead of grams. Recall: to convert from grams to pounds we need to multiply by 0.00220462.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# calculate body mass in lb from conversion factor (0.00220462 lb/g), create new column

penguins_mod <- penguins |>
  mutate(body_mass_lb=body_mass_g*0.00220462)


# then assign it to new object
```
:::




This can be useful for unit conversions. It also be useful for making new calculations based on existing data, for example, the ratio of `bill_length` to `bill_depth`.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins_mod <- penguins_mod |>
  mutate(bill_ratio = bill_depth_mm/bill_length_mm)
```
:::




## `case_when()`

Case when can be used in combination with `mutate` to create a new column with a categorical variable conditional on the values in another column.

For example:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# penguins <- penguins |> 
#   mutate(penguin_length_cat = case_when(bill_length_mm > 50 ~ 'whoa! huge bill!', TRUE ~ '--' ))

# make a new column with a single letter for each penguin species

penguins_mod <- penguins_mod |>
  mutate(spp_abbr = case_when(species=="Adelie" ~ "A",
                              species=="Gentoo" ~ "G",
                              species == "Chinstrap" ~ "C"))


# make a new column with a body mass cutoff that labels penguins below the cutoff as "little" and the ones above it as "BIG"

penguins_mod <- penguins_mod |>
  mutate(size = case_when(body_mass_g >= 5000 ~ "BIG",
                          body_mass_g < 5000 ~ "little"))
```
:::




# Penguin Data Story

I love to play around with data and find little stories, which is what I will be asking you to do more and more as we move through the course material. So I had a little fun with the `palmerpenguins` data and this is what I came up with.
